title: Hosea 2:14–23
context: The LORD continues, turning from the charge to a promise: he will allure her, bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her. Vineyards will be given from there, and the valley of Achor will be a door of hope; she will respond as in the days of her youth, as in the day she came up out of Egypt. In that day she will call him “my husband,” and will no longer call him “my master.” The names of the Baals will be taken out of her mouth. The LORD will make a covenant of safety with the animals of the field, and will break the bow, the sword, and the battle out of the land. The LORD will betroth her to himself forever, in righteousness, justice, loving kindness, compassion, and faithfulness, and she will know the LORD. The heavens and the earth will respond, down to the grain, the new wine, and the oil, and to Jezreel. The LORD will sow her to himself, have mercy on her who had not obtained mercy, and will say to those who were not his people, “You are my people;” and they will say, “You are My God!”

verses.text: “Therefore behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Therefore behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her.” After the visitation of the days of the Baals, the LORD turns: he will allure her, bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her. The wilderness, which had been a picture of want, becomes the place of a tender word. The alluring is the LORD’s own drawing, told without further color.

Arminian readers hear a genuine turning in the LORD’s dealing, a tender speech that comes after judgment, and a drawing that still treats her as one who can be spoken to and can respond.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the alluring, the bringing into the wilderness, and the tender speech as the LORD’s own initiative, his “Therefore” after the charge, the start of the restoration he has purposed.

Shared ground: the LORD will allure her and speak tenderly to her in the wilderness. The unit is a restoration turn, and both traditions read it as his doing.

verses.text: I will give her vineyards from there, and the valley of Achor for a door of hope; and she will respond there as in the days of her youth, and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will give her vineyards from there, and the valley of Achor for a door of hope; and she will respond there as in the days of her youth, and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt.” Vineyards are given from the same wilderness, and the valley of Achor becomes a door of hope. Joshua 7 records Achor as a place of trouble; this verse names it as a door of hope, and the two are not blended. She will respond as in her youth, as in the exodus from Egypt.

Arminian readers hear a hope opened in a valley once marked by trouble, a gift of vineyards, and a response like the first love of the exodus, a turning the LORD makes room for and that she actually makes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the gift of vineyards, the valley of Achor as a door of hope, and the response like the days of youth and of Egypt, as the LORD’s own appointed restoration.

Shared ground: Achor becomes a door of hope, and she will respond as she once did. Joshua 7 stands beside the verse by reference.

verses.text: It will be in that day,” says the LORD, “that you will call me ‘my husband,’ and no longer call me ‘my master.’
verses.arminianNotes:
“It will be in that day,” says the LORD, “that you will call me ‘my husband,’ and no longer call me ‘my master.’” The address changes: she will call him “my husband,” and no longer “my master.” Many readers hear “my master” as the ordinary word also used of the Baals, so that the next verse’s taking away of those names belongs with this new address. The WEB itself sets “my husband” over against “my master.”

Arminian readers hear a new name in her mouth, a marriage word replacing a master word, a change of how she speaks to the LORD that is also a change of how she belongs to him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the new address “my husband,” the end of “my master” and the “says the LORD” as his own promised day, the speech he will bring about in her.

Shared ground: the name she uses for him will change. The next verse will take the Baals’ names out of her mouth.

verses.text: For I will take away the names of the Baals out of her mouth, and they will no longer be mentioned by name.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For I will take away the names of the Baals out of her mouth, and they will no longer be mentioned by name.” The Baals lose their place in her speech. The LORD himself takes the names away, and they will not be mentioned. The new address of the verse before is matched by a cleaned mouth.

Arminian readers hear a real end to the Baal names, a people who will no longer mention what they once burned incense to, and a cleansing of speech that still involves her mouth as the place the names had lived.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the taking away of the Baals’ names from her mouth, and the end of their being mentioned, as the LORD’s own act in that day.

Shared ground: the Baals will no longer be named. The unfaithfulness of the earlier verses is answered in her speech.

verses.text: In that day I will make a covenant for them with the animals of the field, and with the birds of the sky, and with the creeping things of the ground. I will break the bow, the sword, and the battle out of the land, and will make them lie down safely.
verses.arminianNotes:
“In that day I will make a covenant for them with the animals of the field, and with the birds of the sky, and with the creeping things of the ground. I will break the bow, the sword, and the battle out of the land, and will make them lie down safely.” The restoration reaches the creatures and the end of war: a covenant with animals, birds, and creeping things, and the bow, sword, and battle broken, so that they lie down safely. The bow of Israel, broken in judgment in 1:5, is now broken as a weapon of war for the sake of peace.

Arminian readers hear a wide peace, safety in the land, and a covenant that includes even the animals, a promise of rest as real as the earlier want and thirst.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the covenant with the animals, the breaking of bow and sword and battle, and the lying down safely as the LORD’s own appointed peace in that day.

Shared ground: they will lie down safely, and the weapons will be broken out of the land. The safety is the LORD’s gift.

verses.text: I will betroth you to me forever. Yes, I will betroth you to me in righteousness, in justice, in loving kindness, and in compassion.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will betroth you to me forever. Yes, I will betroth you to me in righteousness, in justice, in loving kindness, and in compassion.” The marriage figure is made new: a betrothal that is forever, and that is in righteousness, justice, loving kindness, and compassion. The words are the LORD’s gifts in the bond, not a human achievement. The promise is not turned into a new contrast.

Arminian readers hear a forever betrothal offered to the same people who had been called “not my wife,” a bond in mercy and justice that they can receive as the LORD’s faithful love, real and lasting.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the forever betrothal, and the righteousness, justice, loving kindness, and compassion in which it is made, as the LORD’s own covenant act, sure in his purpose.

Shared ground: he will betroth her to himself forever, and the qualities named are his. Both traditions read this as restoration, not as a new dispute.

verses.text: I will even betroth you to me in faithfulness; and you shall know the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will even betroth you to me in faithfulness; and you shall know the LORD.” Faithfulness is added to the betrothal, and the end is knowledge: she will know the LORD. The knowing is the promised fruit of his faithful bond, the answer to the earlier “she didn’t know” that he had given the grain and the oil.

Arminian readers hear a knowledge of the LORD held out as the aim of the betrothal, a real knowing that answers her old failure to know the giver, and a faithfulness in which she can live.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the betrothal in faithfulness, and the promise “you shall know the LORD.” as his own sure gift, the knowledge he will give in that bond.

Shared ground: she will know the LORD, and the betrothal is in faithfulness. The promise closes the betrothal lines without a new contrast.

verses.text: It will happen in that day, that I will respond,” says the LORD. “I will respond to the heavens, and they will respond to the earth;
verses.arminianNotes:
“It will happen in that day, that I will respond,” says the LORD. “I will respond to the heavens, and they will respond to the earth;” The LORD begins a chain of response: he answers the heavens, and the heavens answer the earth. The day is his, and the first move is his “I will respond”. The sentence runs on into the next verse.

Arminian readers hear a living exchange, heaven and earth answering because the LORD has first responded, a world made fruitful again by his attention, a promise that still invites trust.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the LORD’s “I will respond,” the response to the heavens, and the heavens’ response to the earth, as his own appointed order in that day.

Shared ground: the chain of response begins with the LORD. The next verse will carry it down to the crop and to Jezreel.

verses.text: and the earth will respond to the grain, and the new wine, and the oil; and they will respond to Jezreel.
verses.arminianNotes:
“and the earth will respond to the grain, and the new wine, and the oil; and they will respond to Jezreel.” The chain reaches the grain, the new wine, and the oil — the very gifts once credited to the lovers — and they respond to Jezreel. The name that once marked blood and a broken bow now stands at the end of a fruitful answering. Jezreel can also be heard as a sowing name; the next verse will say, “I will sow her”.

Arminian readers hear the old gifts restored in their true order, answering to Jezreel, a hope for the same name that had been a sentence, now turned toward fruit.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the earth’s response to grain, new wine, and oil, and their response to Jezreel, as the LORD’s appointed fruitfulness, the name now bound to his giving.

Shared ground: the gifts return, and they respond to Jezreel. The name is not dropped; it is taken up into the restoration.

verses.text: I will sow her to me in the earth; and I will have mercy on her who had not obtained mercy; and I will tell those who were not my people, ‘You are my people;’ and they will say, ‘You are My God!’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will sow her to me in the earth; and I will have mercy on her who had not obtained mercy; and I will tell those who were not my people, ‘You are my people;’ and they will say, ‘You are My God!’” The sowing answers Jezreel’s name. Mercy is given to the one who had not obtained mercy, and those who were not his people are told, “You are my people;” and they answer, “You are My God!” Romans 9:25–26 and 1 Peter 2:10 take up this language; see those passages. They stand beside Hosea’s word and are not merged with it.

Arminian readers hear a full reversal of Lo-Ruhamah and Lo-Ammi, a people truly told they are his and truly answering “You are My God!” a restoration as personal as the earlier rupture.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the sowing, the mercy on her who had not obtained mercy, the “You are my people;” and the answering “You are My God!” as the LORD’s own completed reversal, sure in his promise.

Shared ground: the judgment names are turned. Mercy and “my people” are spoken again, and the people confess the LORD as their God.
